_about: range-day-seventeen: the workbench's figures. fpsPerInch is, per caliber, how many feet per second a load's muzzle speed changes for each inch of barrel added (or lost for each inch taken off), from the load's speed from the rifle's own barrel (data/loads.json, muzzleFps); public/builds.js applies it and rounds to the whole foot per second; fpsPerInchWords says each one's basis in plain words for the workbench page. barrels lists, per rifle, the barrel lengths in inches its maker or importer sold for that model, the rifle's own length among them (data/rifles.json, barrelIn); lengths that would make a short-barreled rifle under US federal law (under 16 in without a permanently attached muzzle device) are left out. mounts lists, per scope of the scope collection, the mounts its maker sells, each with the height of the scope's center line over the top of a Picatinny rail; the first is the mount the scope came in (data/sights.json, mount), and a mount at the same height as one already listed is left out. A scope's height over the bore on a rifle is the rifle's rail height (data/rifles.json, scopeMount) plus its mount's. Every figure was read on the date given; this session's network allowed web search but refused page fetches, so each was read from the search engine's indexed text of the page named. range-day-eighteen: short is a mount's name cut to what tells it from the others listed for the same scope, which the workbench shows in its closed picker beside the height (the full name stands under the picker).

5.56x45.estimate: Kept at the game's 25 feet per second per inch. Read from the search engine's indexed text: rifleshooter.com's .223 cut-down from 26 in to 16.5 in, relayed by AccurateShooter (https://bulletin.accurateshooter.com/?p=58189), reported 'an average loss of 25.34 fps per inch', per-load 22.5 to 25.7. Gorilla Ammunition (https://www.gorillaammo.com/?p=224, cited by the game, not re-read this task) gives 34 fps per inch for one 69 gr load between 24 and 16 in. 25 is the rounded cut-down average.

7.62x39.estimate: Kept at the game's 20. Read from the search engine's indexed text of https://www.luckygunner.com/lounge/7-62x39-barrel-length-vs-velocity-what-the-data-shows/: 'on average, they lost 137 fps between the 16.5 and 10.5-inch barrels' (about 23 fps per inch, over a shorter band than the game's rifles use). Velocity loss per inch shrinks as barrels lengthen (same text: losses grow on shorter barrels), so 20 for the 16 to 20 in band.

5.45x39.estimate: No 5.45x39 cut-down test was found (searched ballisticsbytheinch and 'barrel length velocity' for 5.45; nothing indexed). Basis: the nearest small-bore, similar-velocity cut-down, rifleshooter.com's .223 test relayed at https://bulletin.accurateshooter.com/?p=58189, 'average loss of 25.34 fps per inch' (search engine's indexed text), and Hornady's FAQ (https://www.hornady.com/support/faqs/what-would-the-velocity-of-your-ammunition-if-using-a-shorter-barrel), 'approximately 25 to 35 feet per second per inch' (search engine's indexed text).

source.note: University of South Florida honors thesis (B. L. Clark, 2011), 'Effect of Barrel Length on the Muzzle Velocity and Report from a Mosin-Nagant 7.62x54R Rifle': barrel cut from 28.75 in to 16.75 in in 2 in steps, ten rounds per length. Read from the search engine's indexed text: the abstract's method is from the thesis page; the slope 'was 25.658 (Ft/Sec), or 51.316 (Ft/Sec) per barrel length iteration (2 inch cut)' came in a search answer whose result list included https://www.gunboards.com/threads/barrel-length-and-velocity.1246480/ and https://weaponsman.com/effects-of-a-short-barrel/ (the latter quoting one step '2827 fps to 2521 fps'); the thesis PDF itself was not read, so the slope is second-hand. Replaces the game's 20 (Lucky Gunner 7.62x39 basis).

.22 LR.estimate: Over roughly 16 to 27 in, standard-velocity .22 LR gains nothing and may lose a little. Read from the search engine's indexed text: AccurateShooter relaying MDT's test (https://bulletin.accurateshooter.com/tag/barrel-length-velocity), 'with standard rimfire ammunition, the velocity started to decline after 16″ length'; oocities .22 LR page (https://www.oocities.org/CapitolHill/lobby/1221/22lrammo.htm), 'maximum velocities for the .22 LR are usually produced by firearms with barrels between 16" and 18"... friction takes over and actually slows the bullet down'; rec.guns chronograph table (https://groups.google.com/g/rec.guns/c/aEEJy117Ao8), one load about 1,226 fps at 16 in and 1,229 fps at 18.5 in. No CCI Standard Velocity 40 gr figures by barrel length were found. Zero chosen because no source gave a per-inch loss figure to put a negative number on.

source.note: RifleShooter.com's 2019 6.5 Creedmoor cut-down test: average losses of about 21 to 27 feet per second per inch depending on the load; its 2016 test (https://rifleshooter.com/2016/02/6-5-creedmoor-effect-of-barrel-length-on-velocity-cutting-up-a-creedmoor/) averaged 21.8 with a 120 gr bullet and about 16 from 24 to 16 in with a 142 gr bullet. 22, the low end of the 2019 range and the 2016 average, is used. Read from the search engine's indexed text of this page on the date given: this session's network allows web search but refuses page fetches.

Shooting Illustrated: Hornady's 108 gr ELD Match, advertised at 2,750 fps (24-inch test barrel), averaged 2,661 fps from an 18-inch Wilson Combat AR-15, "a reasonable 14.8 fps loss in velocity, for each inch of barrel length"; rounded to 15. Read from the search engine's indexed text of this page on the date given: this session's network allows web search but refuses page fetches.

RifleShooter.com cut a .308 Win barrel from 28 to 16.5 inches with four factory loads: 261 fps lost in all, 22.7 feet per second per inch on average (24.6, 22.8, 20.9 and 22.5 per load; Federal's 168 gr Gold Medal 20.9). Berger's manual gives about 20 per inch from a 24-inch baseline, an MDT test about 25 from 24 to 16 inches. Read from the search engine's indexed text of this page on the date given: this session's network allows web search but refuses page fetches.

fpsPerInchWords.5.56x45: the usual rule for 5.56; a cut-down test of a .223 barrel from 26 to 16.5 inches lost 25 feet per second per inch on average
fpsPerInchWords.7.62x39: the rule the 7.62x39 loads already use; a test of 7.62x39 between 16.5 and 10.5 inches lost about 23 feet per second per inch, and longer barrels lose less per inch
fpsPerInchWords.5.45x39: no test of 5.45x39 was found, so the 5.56 figure is used: a cartridge of the same size and speed; Hornady gives 25 to 35 feet per second per inch for shorter barrels
fpsPerInchWords.7.62x54R: a university test that cut a Mosin-Nagant barrel from 28.75 to 16.75 inches, two inches at a time, found 25.7 feet per second per inch
fpsPerInchWords..22 LR: a standard-speed .22 is fastest from about 16 to 18 inches and gains nothing from a longer barrel, so a longer barrel leaves its speed as it is
fpsPerInchWords.6.5 Creedmoor: cut-down tests of 6.5 Creedmoor barrels lost about 21 to 27 feet per second per inch, depending on the load; 22 is used
fpsPerInchWords.6mm ARC: Hornady's 108 gr match load, rated at 2,750 from a 24-inch test barrel, ran 2,661 from an 18-inch AR-15: about 15 feet per second per inch
fpsPerInchWords.7.62x51: a test that cut a .308 barrel from 28 to 16.5 inches with four factory loads lost 22.7 feet per second per inch on average
